_comment: Compatibility data for the Build yours configurator. microduck/recipe.py and site/build.js both evaluate this file with the same small algorithm; neither holds a combination of its own. 'support' is the single table that says which locomotion each controller supports and through which drive. 'why_not' explains the rest; an entry with 'needs' names a part that would make the row possible. 'rules' add recipe content, or block a selection with a reason and the alternatives that lift the block. Only physical or electrical impossibilities are blocked. The default camera, face and feet are not written here: microduck/recipe.py reads them from config/assembly.json (camera.preset, face, feet). 'manifest_map' and 'report_controller' give the names stl/manifest.json and reports/assembly.json use for a controller or head. Row status: 'report' (read from the reports for the selected controller, camera and head), 'defined', or 'summary' (read from the variants summary when it exists). Sources, assumptions and what has been checked are in docs/status.md, not in the recipe text. Currents are whole mA in multiples of 10.

program_targets.pybricks-ev3: Robot Creator has no way to send a program to an EV3: it shows the program with the manual steps. Put the EV3 MicroPython image on a microSD card, download the .py and copy it with the VS Code EV3 MicroPython extension or scp.
program_targets.ev3dev-python: Robot Creator has no way to send a program to an EV3: it shows the program with the manual steps. Boot ev3dev from a microSD card, download the .py and copy it with the VS Code extension or scp.

why_not.short: Six joints need six position servos; see the crank walker

why_not.reason: Continuous-rotation servos and DC gear motors hold no angle, so they cannot be the biped's leg joints. They are wheel drives.

why_not.reason: The Braccio servos turn 180 degrees. A crank axle or a wheel needs continuous rotation.

set.mechanism: Six-servo biped: left and right hip roll, hip pitch and knee pitch, one hobby servo per joint. No yaw, no ankles. The torso carries the head at the front edge of the deck: a round display as the eyes with a camera board, or the camera mount alone. Four SR431 at the hips, two SR311 at the knees.

assembly: Print the fit pieces first, at 100 percent scale. Try a servo of each size between the rails, both tie paths, the horn on the drill blank, and the camera board in its fit piece.
Print one of each of the other files. Use the horn as a drilling jig on each circular blank.
Centre each servo with the horns off. Strap two SR431 to the torso for hip roll, fit each yoke to its horn with the second SR431 facing outward for hip pitch.
Fit each thigh at its circular end, strap an SR311 at the far end for the knee, and fit the shin to the knee horn, toes forward.
Dry-assemble one leg and sweep it by hand, unpowered, before building the second.

wiring: No camera: the mount at the front of the deck stays empty. The torso listed is the one for the default camera.

The camera board stands in its mount, lower edge on the corner seats, back against the ledges, held by the snap lips, lens the way the toes point and 10 degrees below level. Each board has its own torso file and fit piece.
assembly: Print the camera fit piece before the torso and try the board in it: 0.5 mm is allowed each side and 0.3 mm under the lips.

set.mechanism: Two-motor parallel-crank walker: one motor per side turns two cranks through three 16-tooth gears, and each leg hangs from the two crank tips. Crank radius 12 mm, 24 mm of fore-aft foot travel. Two driven axes.

parts.name: Technic cross axle
parts.note: three per side through the chassis panel; choose lengths after stacking panel, gears, bushes and cranks

parts.name: Technic bushes, pins and liftarms
parts.note: to retain the axles, pivot the legs and hold the motors; build the brackets around the motor in hand

assembly: Print the coupon first, broad face down. Try a cross axle in the keyed hole, a pin in the 4.95 mm hole and a turning axle in the 5.35 mm bearing; the axle must spin freely.
Print one gear and one crank and check them on an axle before printing the rest.
Pass three cross axles through each side panel. Fit a gear to each inside the panel, in one plane; the centre gear idles. Fit a crank to each outer axle outside the panel, both at the same angle.
Pin each leg's two upper holes to the two crank tips, soles inward, the opposite leg half a turn out of phase.
Couple one motor to each side's rear gear axle and hold its housing at two points with Technic beams.
With the motors unplugged, turn each side by hand through a full revolution. Then, body supported, jog one port at a time. Set the phase from the encoder positions before running both sides.

wiring: Pins the driver needs from the controller. TB6612FNG: AIN1, AIN2, PWMA, BIN1, BIN2, PWMB and STBY (seven; five if STBY is tied high and both PWM pins are kept). rules.short: A LEGO motor needs a LEGO motor port
rules.block: A LEGO motor needs a LEGO motor port: the Build HAT, the 51515 hub, the EV3 brick or the BaseX. This drive has none.

wiring: The turning head's parts are drawn for the biped's torso; on this body the pan servo needs its own bracket on the 8 mm grid.

rules.reason: The turning head: a small servo under the front of the deck pans a platform, and the camera sits in a cradle on it.

wiring: Pan by servo, between printed stops. Tilt is set by hand: the cradle turns on one M3 screw and is clamped where it is wanted.
The pan pocket is drawn for an SG90-size case (23 x 12.5 mm body, 32.5 mm across the ears). Measure your servo and try it in fit_sg90_cradle.stl.
The platform takes the servo's horn, or the M5Stack kit's adapter on four holes 8 mm from the axis. Measure the adapter's hole pattern.
The turning-head torso is generated for the UNO Q deck.
assembly: Print fit_sg90_cradle.stl first and check the pan servo in its pocket, the stops and the switch seat. Fit the platform on the horn at mid travel and clamp the tilt by hand.
firmware: Head: not written. The UNO Q agent commands six leg joints; a pan command is not in the line format.

parts.note: a positional 180 degree servo, for example the M5Stack Servo Kit 180. Measure the body against the fit piece.

wiring: One PWM signal for the pan servo, 50 Hz. Restrict the travel in software as well as by the printed stops, and leave cable slack.

firmware: Head: Charmed Labs' EV3 block and EV3 Python class have no servo call, so the EV3 does not command the pan-tilt servos. Try the Pixy2's own pan-tilt program for that.
Head: not written. Under the general firmware the servos are set with setServos(s0, s1), values 0 to 1000 (Charmed Labs general API).

parts.name: M5Stack 360 degree servo for head pan
parts.note: from the Servo Kit 360 or the BALA-C pair. Measure the bracket's hole pattern.

wiring: This servo turns continuously: the pulse sets speed and direction, not angle. Drive it gently towards a stop or add a position sensor; a positional SG90-class servo holds an angle by itself.
Restrict the pan travel mechanically and leave cable slack.
Pan servo signal on the UNO Q: a free PWM pin. Check which pins the Braccio shield leaves free (D2, D7, D8, D13, D20 and D21 are the candidates).
Head servo signal: a spare channel of the servo driver board.
Head servo signal: a Pi GPIO pin with PWM. Under a Build HAT that needs the optional tall header.
Head servo signal: one of the BaseX's two servo outputs, or a Core pin if both drive wheels.
The wheels already use two of these servos. A BALA-C supplies two in all, so the head needs a third.

Omit the two fixed-head pins, couple a vertical motor axle through the centre bearing into the head's cross hole, and support the motor below with Technic beams. Leave cable slack and restrict the pan travel.
firmware: Head: not written.

wiring: LEGO motors mount and couple through Technic axles, pins and beams. Printed holes: 4.95 mm for pins, 5.35 mm for turning axles, keyed cross holes for driven axles, on an 8 mm grid. Print the fit coupon first to set them for your printer.
Pin holes and studs on: the Servo Kit 360 servos have a LEGO-compatible bracket that pins to the grid.

set.mechanism: Fifteen-servo biped in the shape of the Microduck: per leg hip yaw, hip roll, hip pitch, knee and ankle; neck pitch, head pitch, head yaw, head roll and a beak. Eight SR431 and four SR311 from two Braccio kits on the legs and neck, three small 180 degree servos in the head. The eye is a camera board behind the eye ring.

look_a.label: Servo rail of the first shield, 5 V from one Braccio kit supply

look_b.label: Servo rail of the second shield, 5 V from the other Braccio kit supply

wiring: First UNO Q and shield: left hip yaw, hip roll, hip pitch, knee and ankle on M1 to M5, neck pitch on M6. Second: the right leg on M1 to M5, head pitch on M6.
Head yaw, head roll and beak: channels 0 to 2 of a 16-channel PCA9685 servo driver on the first UNO Q's Qwiic connector (I2C, 3.3 V logic), its servo rail on 5 V.
The two boards act as one controller: link them (UART on D0 and D1, crossed, common ground) or drive both from one host.
The small servos must be position servos: the M5Stack Servo Kit 180. The Servo Kit 360 turns continuously and cannot hold a joint.
power: One supply per shield. Do not join the two 5 V rails. Disconnect servo power before the first flash.
The kit supplies cover standing and the simulated walk; for margin use a regulated 5 V 10 A supply per shield, each fused.
Do not run servos or motors from the board's 5 V pin.
firmware: Not written for fifteen joints. The control core in this repository drives six joints on one board.
The joint table is robot/microduck-look/joints.json: names, ranges, servo and output of each joint. Zero and direction are set per horn at calibration.
The model for rehearsal: robot/microduck-look/microduck_look.xml (MJCF) and microduck_look.urdf; python scripts/run_look.py --sim runs it.
assembly: Print the fit pieces first, at 100 percent scale: a servo of each size in its cup, a horn on each plate, the camera board in its seat.
Centre every servo with its horn off. Drop each servo into its cup shaft last until the ears rest on the rim, lead through the slot, one cable tie in the groove.
Trunk: two SR311 into the frame from below (hip yaw). Hang a hip yaw link with its SR431 from each yaw horn (hip roll), then the hip roll link on the roll horn.
Legs: SR431 for hip pitch and knee into each thigh from the inner side; thigh on the hip roll link; shin on the knee horn with its SR431 (ankle); foot on the ankle horn.
Neck: two SR311 in the sleeve, lower horn on the left upright, pivot screw through the right upright. Yoke on the upper horn.
Head: small servos into the carrier (yaw), the lower shell (roll, beak). Carrier on the yoke, lower shell on the carrier with the pivot screw at the front, lower beak on its horn and pivot.
Slide the camera board into the rails behind the eye, fit the face plate and the upper shell, one screw at the back.
Body halves over the frame, two screws each. Boards on the back plate, one above the other, tied through the slots.
Support the robot off the floor for the first power-up and move one joint at a time.
analysis: Assembly test, joint ranges, torques, balance and the simulation: docs/microduck-look.md.

rules.short: The Microduck-look head moves on its own three servos
rules.block: The Microduck-look head has its own yaw, roll and beak servos and a pitching neck. The other head mounts are for the deck of the six-servo biped and the walkers.

assembly: The seat behind the eye is drawn for an Espressif ESP-EYE or an AI-Thinker ESP32-CAM, or for the round display as the eye. This camera does not go behind the face plate: leave the seat empty and carry the camera elsewhere.
For the ESP32-CAM set CAMERA = 'esp32cam' in the design's build.py and print head_face and its fit piece again: the files here seat an ESP-EYE.
The round display as the eye: set EYE = 'display' in the design's build.py and print head_face and its fit piece again. The XIAO's camera then faces backward.

firmware: The camera board lies on its side behind the eye: turn the picture a quarter in software.
